migrationNotes: Spine: a decision-maker is followed from a repeated coin flip to a runaway trolley, adding one idea at each stop (weight outcomes by chance, count harms as negatives, say what the units mean, count lives, add across people) until the method outvotes one person.

lesson.title: Counting consequences

lead.text: Take a different game from the one you were just offered. A spinner pays £30 when it stops on the blue third of the dial, and nothing when it stops anywhere else. Over 300 plays it should land on blue about a hundred times, which pays about £3,000 in all. Shared across the 300 plays, that is £10 a play. You reach the same figure faster by taking one third of £30.

That shortcut is the whole idea. Multiply what each outcome is worth by the chance that it happens, and add the results. When the outcomes are about how well people's lives go, we measure them in units of welfare, a number for how good or bad an outcome is for those affected. The weighted total is the act's expected utility, the value you would average per play if you could repeat the choice many times.

This matters for ethics because of what consequentialists say. Consequentialism is the view that an act is right or wrong according to its outcomes. Outcomes are often uncertain, so a consequentialist ranks acts by their expected utility and favours the highest. The rest of the lesson tests that rule.
Back to the coin game from the start. Heads pays £100 and tails pays nothing, and you can play again and again.

Expected utility earns its keep when you have to choose. Work out the expected utility of each option and take the larger. Here are two programmes. Programme A almost always gives a modest gain: a 90% chance of 60 units of welfare and a 10% chance of 20. Programme B is bolder: a 50% chance of 120 units and a 50% chance of nothing.

afterFigure.text: A comes to 0.9 × 60 + 0.1 × 20 = 56 units. B comes to 0.5 × 120 + 0.5 × 0 = 60 units. So the rule picks B, even though B fails half the time and A almost never does. Someone cautious might still choose A, since they do not want to risk coming away with nothing. The rule itself reports only the average, and a consequentialist who follows it takes the higher one.

lead.text: Compare a sure thing with a gamble. Work out the gamble's expected utility, then see whether it beats the sure 50 units.

reveal.text: You weighed the gamble: 0.6 × 100 + 0.4 × 0 comes to more than the sure 50. An expected-utility maximiser takes the gamble, and a cautious agent might not.

lead.text: So far every outcome has been a gain. Real choices often carry a risk of harm, and the rule handles that by giving a harm a negative value. A harm of 10 units is entered as −10, and it pulls the total down in proportion to its probability.

Consider a clinic deciding whether to offer a new drug. There is a 50% chance that it helps, by 30 units, and a 50% chance that it harms, by 10 units. Weighting each outcome gives 0.5 × 30 = 15 and 0.5 × (−10) = −5. The total is 10 units. Doing nothing is the baseline and scores 0, so on this rule the clinic should offer the drug.

Notice what the rule compares. It never asks whether the drug is good in itself, only whether its expected utility beats the alternatives on the table. The next screen works through a case one step at a time, and the one after leaves a step for you.

steps.headline: A treatment gives 10 units of benefit with probability 0.7 and causes 20 units of harm with probability 0.3. Is it worth giving?

workedSteps.text: Give the harm a negative value.
Weight each outcome by its probability.
Add them. The total is positive, so the treatment beats doing nothing, which scores 0.

steps.headline: A vaccination programme gives 20 units of benefit with probability 0.9 and causes 30 units of harm with probability 0.1. Should it run?

workedSteps.text: Weight the benefit: probability 0.9 times 20 units.
Weight the harm as a negative: probability 0.1 times −30 units.

lead.text: All these units of welfare stand for something, and a consequentialist has to say what. The most influential answer is utilitarianism, developed by Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill. It says that the right act is the one that does the most good for the most people, and that what counts as good is happiness, meaning pleasure and the absence of pain. Mill put it this way: acts are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness. He called this the greatest happiness principle.

Bentham treated all pleasures alike and counted them by amount, such as how intense they are and how long they last. Mill thought that left something out. Reading poetry and eating sweets can feel equally pleasant and still differ in worth, he said, because some pleasures are higher than others. His own line was that it is 'better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied'. Someone who had known both kinds, he argued, would not give up the higher one for any amount of the lower.
Once happiness is the thing to be measured, it can be added up across a whole community. That step is where the trouble begins.

The principle becomes sharp when lives are at stake. In 1967 the philosopher Philippa Foot described a case now known as the trolley problem. A runaway trolley is heading down the main track towards five people who cannot get out of the way. You are standing next to a lever. If you pull it, the trolley turns onto a side track, where it will kill one person instead.

afterFigure.text: A utilitarian treats this as a sum of lives. If you do nothing, five die, and if you pull the lever, one dies. The difference between those two totals shows what the lever changes, and the utilitarian says to choose the option that leaves the most people alive. Most people, asked about this case, agree that pulling the lever is permitted, so here the theory and common opinion line up. Keep that in mind, because the next lesson shows a case where they part.

cases.label: Five ahead, one on the side
Three ahead, one on the side

lead.text: Count only lives, as a utilitarian does. Compare the two options at the lever.

reveal.text: Pulling the lever saves four lives net: five die if you do nothing and one if you pull.

lead.text: The counting rule has a feature that matters more as the numbers grow. It adds welfare across everyone affected, so many small losses can add up to more than one large harm. Philosophers call this aggregation. Suppose a policy gives two people 3 units each and takes 4 units from a third. The total is 6 − 4 = 2, a net gain, even though one person is worse off.

T. M. Scanlon pushed the idea to an extreme. Jones is trapped in a transmitter room and is receiving painful electric shocks. Freeing him means cutting the broadcast of a match that millions are watching, and the repair takes an hour. Each viewer loses a little enjoyment, but there are millions of them.

afterFigure.text: Added up, the viewers' small losses can outweigh Jones's suffering, so a utilitarian who aggregates may leave him where he is. Critics say this ignores the separateness of persons. The viewers' disappointments are never felt by anyone as one great loss, whereas Jones feels his pain alone.

lead.text: Scanlon's case gives a verdict that many people reject. Look at how the theory reaches it, and name the feature responsible.

reveal.text: That feature is aggregation, summing welfare across people, which lets many small losses outweigh one great harm.

lesson.orientation: Rank acts by their expected outcomes, and see where summing welfare across people gives troubling verdicts.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A friend offers you a game. Flip a coin: heads pays £100 and tails pays nothing. You can play as often as you like, and it costs nothing to play. After one flip you hold either £100 or nothing, so a single play tells you very little about the game. Play it a thousand times and a steady picture appears.

Choices outside games work the same way. A doctor deciding whether to give a treatment cannot know whether it will help this patient, but she knows how often it helps patients like this one. A government deciding whether to run a vaccination programme knows the chances and the stakes. Some philosophers say that every act should be judged like this, by the results it can be expected to bring about.

This lesson starts with the coin and learns to weigh chances against stakes. It then applies the same weighing to a runaway trolley, and ends at a case where the method gives a verdict that many people find hard to accept.

intro.promise: By the end you'll rank uncertain acts by their expected utility, and see where adding up welfare across people gives troubling verdicts.

recap.keyIdea: A consequentialist ranks acts by expected utility, weighting every outcome by its probability, with harms as negatives. Adding welfare across people can then outvote one person's great harm.

blocks.text: You weighed a coin game, a vaccination programme and a treatment. You then counted the net lives saved at the lever and met the transmitter room.

recap.nextHook: Counting lives gave a clear answer at the lever. The next lesson puts the same count on a footbridge, where identical arithmetic meets a very different reaction.

questions.prompt: Option B gives a 60% chance of 100 welfare units and a 40% chance of 0. What is its expected utility, in welfare units?
hints: Multiply each outcome's value by its probability.
The failure outcome contributes nothing.
Add the weighted values.
questions.onCorrect: 60 units: 0.6 × 100 plus nothing, which beats the sure 50.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the success value. Weight it by its probability.
That is the weight on failure, not the expected value. Weight the success value by its probability.

questions.prompt: A programme gives 20 units of benefit with probability 0.9 and causes 30 units of harm with probability 0.1. What is its expected utility?
hints: Give the harm a negative value.
Weight each outcome by its probability.
Add the two weighted values.
questions.onCorrect: 15 units: a weighted benefit of 18 less a weighted harm of 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the benefit's weighted value. The harm still has to be subtracted.
Harm counts against the programme. Give it a negative value.

questions.prompt: A runaway trolley will kill five people on the main track unless you pull a lever sending it onto a side track, where it will kill one. Counting lives only, how many more people survive if you pull?
hints: Count the deaths if you do nothing.
Count the deaths if you pull.
Subtract.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Not pulling: five die. Pulling: one dies. 5 − 1 = 4 more survive.

questions.onCorrect: Four more survive: five die if you do nothing, one if you pull.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the deaths if you do nothing. Subtract the death if you pull.
That adds the deaths. You are comparing two options, not totalling them.

questions.prompt: Scanlon's transmitter room: a utilitarian may let Jones suffer an hour of shocks rather than interrupt a broadcast, because millions of small losses add up. Name the feature of utilitarianism that produces this verdict.
hints: Ask how utilitarianism combines the viewers' losses.
The word for adding many small quantities into one total.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Aggregation: summing welfare across people, so many small losses can outweigh one great harm.

questions.onCorrect: Aggregation: many small losses can add up to outweigh one great harm.

misconceptions.feedback: That is part of the theory, but not the feature in question. Ask how the viewers' losses are combined.

questions.prompt: Who wrote that it is 'better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied'?
hints: The line defends higher pleasures within utilitarianism.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Mill, in chapter II of Utilitarianism (1861), defending a distinction between higher and lower pleasures.

questions.onCorrect: Mill, in Utilitarianism (1861), defending higher and lower pleasures.

misconceptions.feedback: Bentham counted the quantity of pleasure. Mill added a distinction between higher and lower.
Kant defends duties that do not depend on outcomes. The line comes from a utilitarian.

questions.prompt: Policy X gives three people +4, +4 and −5 welfare units. Policy Y gives each of them +2. By how many units does Y's total exceed X's?
hints: Add the effects of X across the three people.
Add the effects of Y.
Subtract X's total from Y's.
questions.onCorrect: Three units: Y totals 6 and X totals 3. Aggregation sums welfare across people.

misconceptions.feedback: That is Y's total. Compare it with X's total.
Y's total is the larger one. Subtract X's from Y's.

questions.prompt: A coin-flip game pays £100 on heads and nothing on tails. Played again and again, about how much do you win per play on average, in pounds?
hints: Heads comes up only some of the time.
How often does heads come up over many plays?
Take that share of £100, and add what tails pays.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Heads half the time pays £100, tails half the time pays nothing: 0.5 × 100 = 50.

questions.onCorrect: £50 a play. Weighting each outcome by how often it happens is the idea behind expected utility.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what heads pays, but heads comes up only some of the time.
Tails pays nothing, but heads pays a lot. Weight each by how often it comes up.

questions.prompt: A gamble gives a 50% chance of 10 units and a 50% chance of 20 units. What is its expected utility?
hints: Weight each value by its probability, then add.
questions.onCorrect: Half of 10 plus half of 20: each outcome counts in proportion to its probability.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two values without weighting them. Each counts only half the time.
That is only the lower outcome. Expected utility weights both outcomes.

questions.prompt: Why is the harm written as −20?
hints: What should a harm do to the total?

acceptedIdeas: A bad outcome subtracts from the total.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A bad outcome subtracts from the total.

choices.label: A bad outcome subtracts from the total.
So that the probabilities add to 1.

questions.onCorrect: Harm counts against the act, so it enters with a negative value.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign shows direction, not importance. A harm pulls the total down.
The probabilities already add to 1. The sign is about the value of the outcome.

questions.prompt: Option A gives an 80% chance of 50 units and a 20% chance of −10 units. What is its expected utility?
hints: Give each outcome its probability weight.
The bad outcome has a negative value, so it pulls the total down.
Add the two weighted values.
questions.onCorrect: 38 units. The small chance of harm trims the total, but only in proportion to its probability.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the bad outcome. Weight it and add it as a negative.
That adds the harm instead of subtracting it. The value is negative.
